newsitem.title: HONG KONG: rugby union-HK CELEBRATES RUGBY WITH CHINESE CHARACTERISTICS.
newsitem.headline: rugby union-HK CELEBRATES RUGBY WITH CHINESE CHARACTERISTICS.

text.p: Out with the old and in with the new could have been the motto of the World Cup Sevens, which kicked off on Friday in a blaze of pageantry as Hong Kong marked its last Sevens rugby union tournament under British rule.

The three-day tournament -- incorporating the annual Hong Kong invitation seven-a-side event and only the second World Cup Sevens -- could have been sub-titled "rugby with Chinese characteristics" as organisers sought to draw China into the fold.
China takes over Hong Kong on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule and the organisers sought to add Chinese flavours to the tournament.
Amid intermittent drizzle, local and mainland dance troupes celebrated "fung shui", the ancient Chinese art of geomancy.

Chinese "dragons" accompanied the national flags of the 24 teams competing for the Melrose Cup. Children performed a display of rugby to music to demonstrate the growth of a sport that tournament organisers are billing as one of the region's fastest growing.
And for the first time, a Shanghai television station is beaming highlights into more than 80 million Chinese homes.

China demonstrated its commitment to the sport on Tuesday when a People's Liberation Army team beat members of the British Army's Black Watch regiment in a 10-a-side match in Hong Kong, the same day China was admitted to the International Rugby Football Board. John Abbiss, a businessman and founding member of Hong Kong's rugby union club, was upbeat on the sport's prospects after China takes back the territory.
But Abbiss, who has not missed a tournament since the Hong Kong Sevens started in 1975, was more optimistic than Singapore oil company executive Craig Hill, who has attended five of the tournaments.
Hill assembled a group of friends from around the world to watch the last Sevens before the handover.
But the tradition of the Hong Kong Sevens was not far beneath the surface of this year's packaging, and the event drew its usual assemblage of painted faces, strange hats and even stranger costumes.
Even some of the territory's workaholic businesspeople played truant to watch South Africa pummel Argentina or New Zealand steamroller Japan.
England will be seeking to retain the Melrose Cup, named after the Scottish club credited with the game's invention.

Bars and nightclubs were rolling out the barrels to prepare for all-night visits from revellers seeking to slake a thirst generated by an all-day orgy of meat pies, chips and curry -- the staples of the Sevens.
The 15,000 visitors for the event are expected to spend around HK$7,000 (US$900) each during their stay.
